extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, news organisations, media researchers, and policymakers interested in public trust in news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and survey-derived criteria for what members of the public say matters when deciding which news outlets to trust, based on a 47-market survey and qualitative work. Intended to inform how news organisations can evaluate and build public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: They have a long history
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a news outlet has a long history (longevity/reputation) is one of eight factors asked about in the survey that people say may influence which outlets they trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes this is not necessarily an editorial measure of trustworthiness but is nevertheless important to many respondents. It typically ranks below transparency, high standards, and fairness in importance, and shows more cross-country variation than those core values.

rubrics_metrics.name: They have high journalistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived existence of high journalistic standards at an outlet (quality of reporting, verification, editorial judgment) is one of the eight survey factors respondents can identify as influencing trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter highlights this as a core value that many journalists associate with trustworthiness and one of the top factors respondents name across markets. The authors note limits to what individuals can learn about specific outlets’ standards, so perception matters; discrepancies on charts (e.g., corrected figures) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: They are too negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an outlet is perceived as 'too negative' (tone/attitude of coverage) is one of the eight survey factors that may reduce trust in a news outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor is included because respondents sometimes cite negativity as a reason to distrust outlets. It is not framed as a pure editorial standard but as a perception that shapes trust for some audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: They are biassed
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived bias in reporting (freedom from bias) is one of the eight survey factors respondents can select as important when deciding which outlets to trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom from bias is emphasised as a central, journalist-valued dimension of trustworthiness and among the factors most frequently highlighted by respondents across markets. The report also stresses that perceived bias often intertwines with political context and partisan attacks on media.

rubrics_metrics.name: They exaggerate or sensationalise
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an outlet is perceived to exaggerate or sensationalise stories is an explicit survey factor influencing trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoiding exaggeration and sensationalism is grouped with other journalistic-quality factors (standards, bias, transparency) that respondents frequently cite as important for trust. The report treats this as a perceptual attribute that can hurt trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: They are transparent about how the news is made
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived transparency about newsgathering and editorial processes is one of the eight trust factors respondents were asked about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency is repeatedly called out as a core factor that ranks highly across countries and demographic groups; the chapter notes there is less cross-country variation in emphasis on transparency than for many other factors. Because transparency is visible to audiences, it is both a standard journalists value and a practical lever for building trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Their values are the same as mine
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived values-alignment between the outlet and the respondent is one of the eight survey factors that can influence trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that although some outlets’ perceived values matter to individuals, across all markets this factor is far less frequently mentioned as decisive than transparency, high standards, and fairness. Political alignment can influence trust for particular brands/countries but, at an aggregate level, values-alignment seldom outranks the core journalistic factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: They represent people like me fairly
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether respondents feel an outlet represents people like them fairly (fairness/representation) is one of the eight survey factors influencing trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness — specifically representation of ‘people like me’ — is identified as among the factors most frequently underlined as important. The report also finds groups such as more affluent, higher-educated, older, and more right-leaning respondents are especially likely to insist on the importance of being represented fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust is primarily a matter of perception (distinction between trust and trustworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The report emphasises that public trust is not identical to actual trustworthiness: people may trust institutions that are not trustworthy and distrust ones that are. What matters for media organisations is people’s perceptions of trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing trust as a 'social fact', the chapter stresses that perceptions have real-world consequences for whether audiences believe, engage with, and rely on news. This implies evaluative focus should include measuring public perceptions (surveys, qualitative research) as well as editorial practices, and recognising limits on what audiences can learn about internal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different parts of the public require different approaches; show you live up to expectations (product vs communications)
rubrics_metrics.description: The report argues that securing trust requires tailored strategies: many people know what matters (transparency, standards, bias, fairness) but some large groups (e.g., those who 'don’t know' their political orientation or are not interested in politics) trust the news less and are less sure about what would make them trust outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both an evaluative and prescriptive criterion: outlets should measure trust across audience segments (age, education, income, political interest) and decide whether low trust is a 'product problem' (news isn’t delivering what audiences expect) or a 'communications problem' (audiences are unaware that the outlet meets expectations). The chapter highlights tailoring engagement to distant or politically disengaged groups to earn trust over time.
